passages.title: The sky and earth submit as judgement dawns
passages.tafsir:
# The sky and earth submit as judgement dawns (84:1–6)

This passage is the doorway of Sūrat al-Inshiqāq: two vast cosmic scenes — the sky splitting, the earth stretched flat and emptied — each sealed with the same refrain of obedience, and then a sudden, personal turn: *O man, you are labouring on towards your Lord, and you will meet Him.* What binds the six ayat together is a single argument. The heavens and the earth, immense as they are, submit without resistance when their Lord commands; and you, small as you are, are already travelling toward that same Lord whether you realise it or not. Ibn Kathir says of the opening words simply: "This refers to the Day of Judgement" — and the heading he gives the whole scene, "Splitting the Heavens asunder and stretching the Earth forth on the Day of Resurrection," places the sky's splitting and the earth's stretching alike on that Day.

## Two scenes, one refrain (ayat 1–5)

**Ayah 1** opens with the sky bursting open — the event that gives the sūrah its name (*inshiqāq*, splitting). **Ayah 2** then says something remarkable about it: *wa-adhinat li-rabbihā wa-ḥuqqat* — "and it listens to and obeys its Lord, and it must do so." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on both verbs. *Adhinat* literally means "it listens", but here listening includes obeying — the sky hears the command to split apart and complies at once. *Ḥuqqat* means it was only right that it should: the obligation to obey was always upon it. Ibn Kathir explains why: the command of its Lord is great and "cannot be rejected, nor overcome. Rather it overpowers everything and everything is submissive to it."

**Ayat 3–4** turn from above to below. The earth is *muddat* — stretched forth. The word *madda*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, means to stretch, spread, expand out. Maʿārif cites a report from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh that the Prophet ﷺ said the earth will on that Day be stretched out like leather into a smooth plain, with just enough space for every human being ever born to place his feet — for on the Day of Resurrection every individual from the beginning of creation until its end will stand there at once (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this as transmitted by Hakim with a good chain of authorities, via Mazhari). Maʿārif adds that this new earth prepared for the Gathering (*Ḥashr*) will have neither caves nor mountains, neither buildings nor trees — flat and smooth, with room for the former and the latter generations together.

Then the earth *casts out all that was in it and becomes empty*. Ibn Kathir, citing Mujahid, Sa'id and Qatadah, says it throws out the dead inside it and empties itself of them. Maʿārif widens the picture: with one convulsion the earth will throw up whatever its belly contains — natural treasures, buried treasures, mines, and the bodies of the dead down to their scattered particles. Nothing entrusted to it stays hidden.

**Ayah 5** then repeats the refrain of ayah 2, word for word, now for the earth: it listens, it obeys, and it must. The repetition is the passage's heartbeat. Sky above, earth below — the entire created frame answers its Lord the moment He speaks.

**How do sky and earth "obey"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a subtle point here. Divine commands are of two kinds: the *legislated* command — the law given to beings with intellect, humans and jinn, who remain free to obey or rebel, and are thereby divided into believer and unbeliever; and the *cosmic, destined* (*takwīnī*) command — the decree that runs through the universe by force, which no creature, pious or impious, can deviate from in the least. Which kind is meant here? Maʿārif offers both possibilities: it may be that on that Day Allah will endow the sky and the earth with sense and perception like humans and jinn, so that they receive His command and choose, of their own volition, to act on it; or the ayah may refer to the irresistible cosmic command, taken figuratively. Maʿārif judges that the wording — "it *listens* to its Lord, and it ought to" — sits closer to the first meaning, while allowing the second. We affirm what the ayah says without pressing further: the sky will hear and obey, in the way its Lord knows.

## The turn to man (ayah 6)

After five ayat about the cosmos, the address suddenly narrows to a single listener: *yā ayyuhā l-insān* — O man! The key word is *kādiḥ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *kadḥ* means to exert one's efforts fully — relentless, straining toil. The ayah is a statement of fact before it is a warning: every human being, believer or unbeliever, is by nature a labourer. Maʿārif observes that the good person toils by lawful means for his livelihood, and even the thief, the robber and the cheat apply mind and muscle to reach their goals. No one is idle. And — here is the ayah's disclosure — all of that striving, whether the striver knows it or not, is stations of one long journey whose terminus is fixed: *ilā rabbika*, "towards your Lord." Every road of effort ends at death, and death is arrival in His presence. This, Maʿārif says, is a statement of reality none can deny.

**"…and you will meet" — meet what?** The final word, *fa-mulāqīh*, carries a pronoun the scholars read two ways, and both readings are in the sources. Ibn Kathir gives the first: you will meet *it* — your deed, the good and evil you worked. As proof he cites what Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded from Jabir, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Jibril said, "O Muhammad! Live how you wish, for verily you will die; love what you wish, for verily you will part with it; and do what you wish, for verily you will meet it." The second reading refers the pronoun back to "your Lord": you will meet *Him*, and He will repay you for your work. Ibn Kathir remarks that the two views are really connected — and Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, recorded by al-ʿAwfī, joins them in one sentence: "Whatever deed you do, you will meet Allah with it, whether it is good or bad." You meet your Lord, and you meet Him carrying your deeds.

**Why a reckoning at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a piece of quiet reasoning. In this world the distinction between good and evil striving is invisible in the results: an honest man may labour a month for what a looter seizes overnight. If there were no time of reckoning, the good and the bad would end up equal — which is contrary to reason and justice. So the meeting announced in ayah 6 is not arbitrary terror; it is the necessary moment when the consequences of every kind of toil are finally told apart. Maʿārif notes that the verses that follow depict the consequences of the two — the good and the bad — separately.

## Living with these ayat

Two practical notes flow straight from the sources. First, this sūrah contains a **prostration of recitation**. It is reported from Abu Salamah that Abu Hurayrah, leading the prayer, recited *idhā s-samāʼu nshaqqat* and prostrated, then explained that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had prostrated at its recitation — recorded by Muslim and An-Nasa'i on the authority of Malik. And Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Rafiʿ that he prayed the night prayer with Abu Hurayrah, who recited this sūrah and prostrated; when Abu Rafiʿ questioned him about it, Abu Hurayrah replied: "I prostrated behind Abul-Qasim (the Prophet ﷺ), and I will never cease prostrating during its recitation until I meet him." There is something fitting in it: a passage about the sky and earth submitting to their Lord is answered by the reciter putting his own face on the ground.

Second, the ayah's realism about effort is itself the counsel. Since toil is unavoidable — everyone is *kādiḥ* — the only real question is its direction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes on precisely this: man still has the chance, while he lives, to redirect his hard work so that it not only meets his legitimate needs in this world but secures the eternal pleasure of the Hereafter. The sky and the earth will obey when the command comes, because they must. The believer is invited to obey now, while obedience is still a choice.

passages.title: The two records: easy reckoning or blazing ruin
passages.tafsir:
## The two records

The sūrah has just told every human being that he is journeying toward his Lord and will meet what he did. Ayat 7–15 now show that meeting from both sides: one person receives his record in his right hand, is reckoned gently, and goes back to his family in joy; the other receives it from behind his back, cries out for his own destruction, and enters a blazing Fire. What binds the passage together is the *book* — the written record of deeds — and the quietly devastating point that the difference between the two endings was decided by how each man lived with the thought of this Day.

## The easy reckoning — and what "easy" really means

In ayah 7 the record is placed *in the right hand*, and ayah 8 promises "an easy reckoning" (*ḥisāban yasīrā*). Ibn Kathir explains what this ease consists of: it is "easy without any difficulty" — the person will **not be investigated for all the minute details of his deeds** — "for verily, whoever is reckoned like that, he will certainly be destroyed."

That startling last clause comes straight from the Sunnah. Imam Ahmad recorded from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever is interrogated during the reckoning, then he will be punished." 'A'ishah objected: but has Allah not said, *"He surely will receive an easy reckoning"*? The Prophet ﷺ replied that the ayah is not speaking of interrogation at all, but of the **presentation** (*al-ʿarḍ*): "Whoever is interrogated during the Reckoning on the Day of Judgement, then he will be punished." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was also recorded by Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Jarir; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from the Sahih of Bukhari.

The distinction matters enormously. The believer's deeds *will* be laid out before Allah — nothing is hidden or waived — but, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, by virtue of his faith his actions will merely be presented, not scrutinised line by line and demanded of him. No one survives an audit of the minute details; the "easy reckoning" is Allah's mercy in not conducting one. This is the passage's first great consolation: salvation on that Day is not passing a perfect examination, but being spared the cross-examination altogether.

## "He will return to his family in joy"

Ayah 9 completes the picture: *wa-yanqalibu ilā ahlihi masrūrā* — he turns back to his family *masrūr*, which Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak explain as "happy and delighted by what Allah has given him." But who are "his family"?

Ibn Kathir, citing Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak, says it means his family **in Paradise**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Qurtubi, records both interpretations the commentators have offered: it may refer to the ḥūrs (the maidens of Paradise) who will be his household there, or it may refer to his own worldly family present on the Plain of Gathering — so that the moment he learns of his success, he hurries to them, "according to the custom of this life," to share the good news. Both readings preserve the ayah's warmth: the reward is not only escape from punishment but a homecoming.

## The record behind the back

Ayah 10 turns to the other man — and the wording is chillingly physical. He is not simply handed his book in the left hand; it is given to him *from behind his back*. Ibn Kathir explains the scene: he will receive his book in his left hand, **behind his back, while his hand is bent behind him**. (The translation's "in their left hand" and the ayah's "behind his back" describe the same reception.)

His response, in ayah 11, is to "invoke destruction" — he cries out for *thubūr*, which Ibn Kathir glosses as loss and destruction. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the horror of this: such people **will desire death and destruction under the impression that this might end their misery — but it will not be possible for them to die**. And instead of annihilation, ayah 12 gives him the Fire: "he shall enter a blazing Fire, and made to taste its burning."

## Two joys — the mirror at the heart of the passage

Notice a single repeated word in the ayat themselves. The saved man returns to his family *masrūrā* — in joy (ayah 9). And why is the other man ruined? "Verily, he was among his people *masrūrā*" — in joy (ayah 13). The same word, in the same phrase about family, carries opposite verdicts.

Ibn Kathir explains the difference: the doomed man's joy was heedless joy — "he did not think about the consequences, nor feared what was in front of him. His light happiness will be followed by long grief." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops the contrast with the believers, quoting their own words in Paradise from Sūrah At-Tur, ayah 26: *"Indeed we were afraid (of Allah's punishment) when we were amidst of our family."* The believers also lived among their families, also knew pleasure and comfort — but at every moment of it they remained conscious and even anxious about the Hereafter. Each group's end, Maʿārif observes, is fitted exactly to its posture in the world: those who enjoyed their families oblivious of the reckoning meet grief; those who enjoyed them while fearing the reckoning receive their families and their joy back, this time forever. The Qur'an is not condemning happiness — it is asking what your happiness is built on.

## "He thought he would never return"

Ayah 14 names the root of the whole disaster: *innahu ẓanna an lan yaḥūr* — "he thought that he would never return." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others explain: he believed he would not return to Allah, that Allah would not bring him back to life after his death. Denial of resurrection is what made his heedless joy possible; a man who expects no audit keeps no accounts.

Ayah 15 answers him in one word before the sentence even begins: *Balā* — "Yes!" Yes, he will return. "Verily, his Lord has been ever beholding him" (*baṣīrā*). Ibn Kathir draws out both edges of this: Allah will certainly repeat his creation just as He began it, and He will repay him for his deeds, good or bad — for He was ever watchful of him all along, All-Knowing and All-Aware. We affirm this as the ayah states it: Allah truly sees His servant, always has, in a manner befitting His majesty. The man imagined his life was unobserved and his story would simply end; in reality every moment of it was witnessed, and the record now in his hands proves it.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with two concrete orientations. First, hope in the right measure: aim not to survive an interrogation — no one would — but hope for the *ʿarḍ*, the merciful presentation, which Allah grants by virtue of faith. Second, the lesson Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly: a believer should not be so immersed in the comforts of this life that he becomes oblivious of the reckoning. Enjoy your family and your blessings — the righteous of At-Tur, ayah 26 did — but never let ease erase the memory of the Day when the book changes hands. Whether it arrives in the right hand or from behind the back is being written now.

passages.title: Oaths by twilight, night, and moon: stage by stage
passages.tafsir:
# The Oaths of the Evening Sky — and the Journey They Prove

This passage is a single oath-sequence. In ayat 16–18 Allah swears by three scenes of the evening sky — the fading twilight, the night and all it gathers in, and the moon grown full — and in ayah 19 He delivers the point the oaths exist to drive home: *"You will certainly pass from one state to another."* What binds the four ayat together is one idea: nothing in creation stands still, and neither do you. In Ibn Kathir's tafsir this discussion comes under the heading "Swearing by the Various Stages of Man's Journey" — the sky at dusk is made a witness against the person who imagines his own life has no direction and no destination.

## Why swear by these three things?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the logic of the selection. Each thing sworn by is itself caught in transition, and each transition transforms the world of man:

- **The twilight (ash-shafaq, ayah 16)** is the red glow lingering in the west after sunset — the harbinger of a massive change, as light drains away and "a flood of darkness is setting in."
- **The night (ayah 17)** then completes that change.
- **What the night "gathers" (also ayah 17)** — everything that scatters abroad by day and retreats home at dusk: people to their houses, animals to their habitats, birds to their nests, merchandise piled up in one place.
- **The moon (ayah 18)** does not even stay one shape: it appears as a fine sliver, grows night after night, and only "when it ittasaq" — when it has gathered its light — stands full.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties these oaths back to the sūrah's earlier announcement in ayah 6, "you have to work hard constantly to reach your Lord": the four phenomena "bear evidence to the subject in the complement of the oath, that is, the condition of man never remains the same at all times." The evening sky is not decoration here; it is the proof.

## The words themselves

**Ash-shafaq.** Ibn Kathir gathers an impressive roll-call — ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUbadah bin As-Samit, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn ʿUmar, Malik, and others — all saying that ash-shafaq is "the redness in the sky." (Abdur-Razzaq records from Abu Hurayrah a view that it is the whiteness, and Mujahid placed the redness before sunset rather than after, but the redness after sunset is, as Ibn Kathir puts it, what is well known with the scholars of the Arabic language.) The linguists pin it down: Al-Khalil bin Ahmad said it is the redness that appears from sunset until the time of ʿIshaʼ, so that when it fades one says "the shafaq has disappeared"; Al-Jawhari called it the remaining light of the sun at the beginning of the night; ʿIkrimah said simply, it is "what is between al-Maghrib and al-ʿIshaʼ."

Ibn Kathir then cites the hadith in the **Sahih of Muslim**, from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The time of al-Maghrib is as long as ash-shafaq has not disappeared."* The very glow Allah swears by marks the time of a daily prayer: Maghrib's window lasts as long as that redness lasts. Ibn Kathir takes this hadith as proof that Al-Khalil and Al-Jawhari defined the word correctly.

**Wasaqa and ittasaq — one root, two ayat.** The two verbs in ayat 17 and 18 come from the same root, whose primitive sense, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is "to pile, gather, heap up." Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Al-Hasan and Qatadah all explained "what it wasaqa" as "what it gathers" — Qatadah specified "the stars and animals it gathers," and ʿIkrimah said it is what the night "drives into due to its darkness, because when it is nighttime everything goes to its home." Then the moon *ittasaq*: it "gathers" too — but what it gathers is its own light. Ibn ʿAbbas said, "when it comes together and becomes complete"; Al-Hasan, "when it comes together and becomes full"; Qatadah, "when it completes its cycle" — the full moon of the fourteenth night, the *badr kāmil*. Ibn Kathir himself draws the thread between the two verbs: these statements refer to the moon's light when it is completed and becomes full, "as the idea was initiated with 'The night and what it gathers.'" So the night gathers the world into itself, and the moon gathers light into itself.

## Ayah 19: "stage after stage"

The oath resolves in ayah 19: *la-tarkabunna ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq*. The word *ṭabaq* means a stage; the verb *la-tarkabunna*, from *rukūb*, means "to mount" — you will certainly mount up, stage upon stage, never resting in one condition.

Ibn Kathir records that **Al-Bukhari** relates from Mujahid that Ibn ʿAbbas said of this ayah: "Stage after stage. Your Prophet ﷺ has said this." The early commentators then unfold what those stages are. ʿIkrimah read it through the arc of a single life: "Weaned after he was breastfeeding, and an old man after he was a young man." Al-Hasan Al-Basri read it through the reversals inside a life: "Ease after difficulty, difficulty after ease, wealth after poverty, poverty after wealth, health after sickness, and sickness after health." Both are true, and together they cover a human existence completely — the stages you climb in order, and the states that overturn without warning.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the whole ascent in detail: from the joining of sperm and egg, to the clot, the lump of flesh, the bones clothed in flesh, the breathing-in of the soul; from the womb to the mother's milk; from crawling to walking to speech; from play to study, from youth to marriage and household, and then the slow surrender of strength, old age, and death. "All this happens in full view of everyone. No one dare deny this." And here is the passage's cutting edge: the heedless person assumes the grave is the last stage. Revelation corrects him — the grave, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, "is merely a waiting-room" before an enormously larger world yet to come, where the final examination will be conducted and the final stage of his life will be determined: eternal comfort and pleasure in the remembrance of Allah, or eternal perdition. The commentary anchors this in the Qurʼan's own refrain: "Surely, to your Lord is the return" (96:8) and "you have to work hard constantly to reach your Lord" (84:6). The stages do not trail off; they arrive somewhere — at your Lord.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a narration recorded by Abu Nuʿaim from Jabir Ibn ʿAbdullah, that the Prophet ﷺ indicated these verses remind the unmindful person of his creation and the vicissitudes of his life, and instruct him to reconsider his position and its consequences while there is still time, and to prepare for the next life.

## Living under this oath

If every sunset is a proof that your state is changing, then the believer's posture is that of a traveller passing through stages, not a settler. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly this conclusion, citing the Prophet's ﷺ counsel: *"Be in this world as though you are a stranger or a wayfarer."* A wise person treats walking, sleeping, waking, standing and sitting as ground being covered on a journey whose end is standing before Allah — and cultivates in this life for the next. The passage asks nothing exotic of you: only that when you see the red glow fade tonight, you read it the way Allah swears it should be read — as evidence that you, too, are moving, stage after stage, toward your Lord.

passages.title: Why they refuse the Quran, and the two ends
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the closing argument of Surah al-Inshiqaq. After swearing by the twilight, the night and what it envelops, and the full moon that every human being travels "from stage to stage" toward his Lord (ayat 16–19), Allah asks the question the whole surah has been building toward: *given all of this, what is the matter with them that they do not believe?* (ayah 20). The passage then names what actually stands behind their refusal (ayat 22–23), announces its consequence (ayah 24), and ends the surah with the shining exception — the believers and their never-ending reward (ayah 25). Refusal and faith, torment and reward: the two ends of the journey.

## A question that follows an argument

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents these verses as the *conclusion* drawn from the oaths that precede them: "Therefore, the verse concludes: So, what has happened to them that they do not believe...?" Allah had sworn by four phenomena. The first is the twilight — the red glow that remains on the western sky after sunset, the harbinger of a massive change as light disappears and a flood of darkness sets in. The second is the night itself, which completes that change. The third is all that the night envelops: the word *wasaqa* carries the sense of gathering and piling up, so it embraces everything the darkness covers and everything that retreats to its own place at nightfall — human beings to their homes, animals to their habitats, birds to their nests. The fourth is the moon "when it develops at the full": first a fine crescent, then light growing night after night until it becomes the full moon of the fourteenth night. Each oath is a picture of ceaseless change — and so with man: "You shall certainly travel from stage to stage" (ayah 19). Al-Bukhari recorded from Mujahid that Ibn 'Abbas explained this as "Stage after stage," adding, "Your Prophet ﷺ has said this." 'Ikrimah illustrated it: weaned after breastfeeding, an old man after being a young man. Al-Hasan al-Basri widened it: ease after difficulty, wealth after poverty, health after sickness — and back again.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the stages further: from the joining of sperm and egg, to a clot, to flesh and bone, to the soul breathed in; from the womb to the world, from childhood play to youth, marriage and work, then weakening strength, old age, and death. All of this happens "in full view of everyone. No one dare deny this." Yet the heedless person assumes the grave is the last stage — while revelation makes known that the grave is only "a waiting-room" before the vast world where the final examination will be conducted and his eternal station determined. This is the same truth the surah stated earlier: "you have to work hard constantly to reach your Lord" (84:6).

It is against this backdrop that the question of ayah 20 lands: *"So what is the matter with them that they do not believe?"* Ibn Kathir gives the question its force: what prevents them from believing in Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the Last Day?

## The refusal named

Ayah 21 continues the charge: "and when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not bow down." Ibn Kathir explains: what is wrong with them that when Allah's Ayat and His Words are recited to them, they do not prostrate "due to awe, respect and reverence"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it this way: when the Qur'an, "replete with clear guidelines," is recited to them, they do not bow in submission.

Then ayah 22 answers the question of ayah 20: "In fact, the disbelievers persist in denial." Ibn Kathir: "from their mannerism is rejection, obstinacy, and opposition to the truth." Rejection, obstinacy, and opposition are, in his words, part of their very manner.

Ayah 23 then goes to the place arguments cannot reach: "But Allah knows best whatever they hide." Mujahid and Qatadah both explained "mā yūʿūn" as "what they conceal in their chests." Whatever lies behind the public denial, Allah knows it precisely; nothing gathered and stored in the chest escapes Him.

## "Give them good news" of torment

Ayah 24 draws the consequence: "So give them good news of a painful punishment." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning plainly: "inform them, O Muhammad, that Allah has prepared for them a painful torment." Those who refused to believe are handed an announcement of an altogether different kind from the glad tidings the believers receive.

## The exception: the two ends

And then, in the surah's final breath, ayah 25: "But those who believe and do good will have a never-ending reward." Ibn Kathir calls this "a clear exception" and notes its two halves with care: "those who believe" refers to what is in their *hearts*, and "do righteous good deeds" refers to what they do with their *limbs*. Inner conviction and outward action together — the exact opposite of the deniers, whose chests concealed what only Allah knows.

Their reward — in the abode of the Hereafter, as Ibn Kathir notes — is "ghayr mamnūn." The early authorities circled this word from different sides: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Without being decreased"; Mujahid and ad-Dahhak said, "Without measure"; as-Suddi relates that some said it means without end and without decrease. Ibn Kathir sums up: the result of their statements is that the reward is without end, as Allah says elsewhere, "A gift without an end" (11:108). Everything else in the surah has been change — twilight fading, stages passing, life mounting from phase to phase. The one thing declared permanent is the believers' reward. The travel ends; the reward does not.

## The prostration of recitation at this ayah

Ayah 21 raises a practical question the classical scholars discussed at length, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats it carefully.

First, the meaning. The word sajdah literally denotes "to bow" and connotes obedience. In ayah 21 it is not being used in its technical sense of the ritual prostration, but in the sense of bowing in submission — with respect, humility, and humbleness — to the Qur'an as a whole. The proof is the verse itself: it speaks of "the Qur'an" being recited, not one particular verse; if the technical prostration were meant, a prostration would be due at every single verse of the Qur'an, which no one — neither the salaf (the early generations) nor the khalaf (those after them) — has ever held.

Second, the ruling. Is a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilāwah) due when *this* verse is recited? Here the jurists genuinely differed, because the narrations themselves differ. Imam Abu Hanifah held that prostration at this verse is an obligatory duty, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites his evidence: Bukhari recorded from Abu Rafi' that he prayed 'Isha behind Abu Hurayrah, who recited "When the sky will split apart" and prostrated at the relevant verse. When Abu Rafi' asked him about it, Abu Hurayrah replied: "I prostrated at this verse behind Abul Qasim in a salah, and I will never cease prostrating during its recitation until I meet him on the Plain of Gathering." Muslim likewise transmitted from Abu Hurayrah that they prostrated with the Prophet ﷺ at the relevant verses of this surah and of Surah "Iqra' bismi Rabbik."

Some Hanafi jurists even argued from ayah 21 itself, reading "the Qur'an" there as referring specifically to this verse — but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges that reading far-fetched against the clear context, and rests the ruling on the Prophet's ﷺ practice instead. Other narrations indicate the prostration here is not obligatory, and other jurists held accordingly.

Qurtubi preserves a touching illustration of how seriously the scholars took both the ruling and the unity of the community. Ibn al-'Arabi held that prostration at this verse is obligatory — yet he lived among people whose custom, probably following an Imam who did not hold it obligatory, was not to prostrate here. So whenever he led the congregational prayer he simply avoided reciting Surah al-Inshiqaq: to omit the prostration would, in his view, be sinning; to perform it would strike his congregation as an unnecessary act. He chose not to split the community unnecessarily. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical thread through the whole passage. If life is stages mounting toward Allah, then "a wise person should treat himself in this world as a traveller and prepare himself for the next world" — as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Be in this world as though you are a stranger or a wayfarer." And it cites a narration recorded by Abu Nu'aim from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah that the Prophet ﷺ indicated these verses remind the heedless person of his creation and the vicissitudes of his life, and instruct him to reconsider his position and its consequences while there is still time, and to prepare for the next life. Yet, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, despite these clear guidelines there are people who never desist from their heedlessness.

Two responses to the recited Qur'an, two ends. One heart hears it and will not bow — and conceals within itself what only Allah knows. Another believes with the heart, works with the limbs, and bows the moment the ayah of prostration passes his lips, as Abu Hurayrah vowed to do until the Day he meets his Prophet ﷺ on the Plain of Gathering. The surah leaves the reader standing between a painful torment and a reward that will never diminish — and asks him, in effect, its own question: what is the matter with us, that we do not believe?
